nodes.text: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) are a class of iterative implicit probabilistic models that generalize DDPMs via a family of non-Markovian forward (inference) processes which share the same training objective, enabling more efficient sampling.
nodes.evidence: We generalize DDPMs via a class of non-Markovian diffusion processes that lead to the same training objective.

nodes.text: The DDPM training objective L_gamma depends only on the marginals q(xt|x0), not on the joint q(x1:T|x0); since many inference joints share the same marginals, alternative non-Markovian inference processes can be used with the same trained model.
nodes.evidence: the DDPM objective in the form of L only depends on the marginals q(xt|x0), but not directly on the joint q(x1:T|x0).

nodes.text: A family of non-Markovian inference processes indexed by sigma is constructed; the variational objective J_sigma for any sigma is equivalent (up to a constant) to the DDPM surrogate objective L_gamma, so a pretrained DDPM can be reused without retraining for any choice of sigma.
nodes.evidence: Theorem 1. For all sigma > 0, there exists gamma in R^T>0 and C in R, such that J = L + C.

nodes.text: Setting sigma_t = 0 for all t makes the generative process deterministic (no random noise term), yielding the implicit model named DDIM, which is trained with the DDPM objective despite the forward process no longer being a diffusion.
nodes.evidence: we note another special case when sigma_t = 0 for all t; ... the coefficient before the random noise becomes zero. The resulting model becomes an implicit probabilistic model

nodes.text: When sigma_t takes a specific value matching the DDPM forward variance, the non-Markovian forward process becomes Markovian and the generative process recovers DDPM, so DDPM is a special case of the generalized family.
nodes.evidence: When sigma_t = sqrt((1-alpha_{t-1})/(1-alpha_t))... the forward process becomes Markovian, and the generative process becomes a DDPM.

nodes.text: Accelerated generation samples over a sub-sequence (trajectory) tau of length S << T of the original latent variables, since the L1 objective does not depend on the specific forward procedure as long as q(xt|x0) is fixed, requiring no change to training.
nodes.evidence: we may also consider forward processes with lengths smaller than T, which accelerates the corresponding generative processes without having to train a different model.

nodes.text: The DDIM update can be rewritten to resemble Euler integration of an ODE, and this ODE is equivalent to a special case of the concurrent probability flow ODE of Song et al. (corresponding to a continuous-time analog of DDPM).
nodes.evidence: our ODE is equivalent to a special case of theirs (which corresponds to a continuous-time analog of DDPM).

nodes.text: DDIM produces high quality samples 10x to 50x faster in wall-clock time than DDPM, allowing a trade-off of computation for sample quality.
nodes.evidence: DDIMs can produce high quality samples 10x to 50x faster in terms of wall-clock time compared to DDPMs

nodes.text: DDIM has superior sample quality to DDPM when sampling is accelerated by 10x to 100x.
nodes.evidence: DDIMs have superior sample generation quality compared to DDPMs, when we accelerate sampling by 10x to 100x using our proposed method.

nodes.text: DDIM samples exhibit a 'consistency' property absent in DDPMs: samples generated from the same initial latent with chains of different lengths share similar high-level features, enabling semantically meaningful interpolation in latent space.
nodes.evidence: if we start with the same initial latent variable and generate several samples with Markov chains of various lengths, these samples would have similar high-level features.

nodes.text: Unlike DDPM, the deterministic DDIM ODE can be reversed to encode observations x0 into latents xT, providing latent representations useful for downstream applications and low-error reconstruction.
nodes.evidence: unlike DDPM, we can use DDIM to obtain encodings of the observations (as the form of xT), which might be useful for other downstream applications

nodes.text: DDIM closes the efficiency gap between DDPMs and GANs, motivated by DDPM requiring thousands of sequential steps (e.g. ~20 hours for 50k 32x32 images) while a GAN needs a single network pass.
nodes.evidence: To close this efficiency gap between DDPMs and GANs, we present denoising diffusion implicit models (DDIMs).
